title: What to Say When Someone Twists Your Words
summary: When someone manipulates or twists your statement in a meeting, saying "what I meant was" can make it sound like you are backtracking on something you never said. Instead, use the "Same Words" technique by repeating your statement using the exact same phrasing you originally used. This clarifies your position and maintains control without sounding defensive.
key_points: Avoid saying "No, no, what I meant was...", as it sounds like you are taking back your statement even though you never said their version.
Use the "Same Words" technique: repeat your point using the exact same words you used the first time.
Example response: When someone says, "So what you're saying is the sales team isn't doing its job," respond with: "No. What I said was, 'we're losing too many deals before the contract gets signed.'"
Using the exact same words demonstrates that you meant what you said and are standing by your original statement.
If someone twisted your words on purpose, repeating your exact original phrase highlights the contradiction immediately.
If someone genuinely misunderstood, hearing the exact statement again helps them realize what you actually said.

Post Text:
Here’s what to say when someone tries to twist your words. You have to correct it, so you don’t get blamed for something you never said. But it’s hard to know the right way to do it without getting into an argument. I taught communication at Duke and Columbia, and here is what to say. You can follow me for more on becoming a better communicator.

Transcript:
Here's what to say when someone twists your words so you can regain control of your message without sounding defensive. It is so frustrating when someone tries to manipulate your words, and it's essential to correct it so you don't get blamed for something you never said. Maybe you're in a meeting and you say, "We're losing too many deals before the contract gets signed." Your colleague says, "So what you're saying is the sales team isn't doing its job." They've turned your point into something you never said, and their version makes you sound like a jerk. That is a trap. I'm a former presidential campaign spokesperson, and here is what to say. A lot of people jump in with, "No, no, what I meant was," because you want to clear it up fast. But "what I meant" sounds like you're taking it back, and you didn't say it in the first place. Instead, use what I call the Same Words technique. Here's how it works: You repeat your point in the exact same words you used the first time. So when they say, "So what you're saying is the sales team isn't doing its job," you say, "No. What I said was, 'we're losing too many deals before the contract gets signed.'" It works because using the same words shows that you meant what you said and you're standing by it. If they were twisting it on purpose, that shows up right away because your point and their version don't sound anything alike. And if they genuinely misunderstood you, hearing it again helps them grasp that you didn't mean it that way. So, the next time someone twists your words in a meeting, try the Same Words technique, and follow me for more on becoming a better communicator.
